extracted.intended_audience: Public Information Officers, incident information staff, and trainees in emergency/incident management
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for Public Information Officers to plan and conduct community relations, communications (one-way and two-way), news conferences, and to prepare for and manage special situations (‘incidents-within-an-incident’) during emergencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: PIO primary community relations functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep individuals and organizations in affected communities informed about and involved in the incident and incident management activities; Enable individuals and organizations in affected communities to express their concerns, needs, and issues to the IMT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the two main functions identified for Public Information Officers and other incident personnel; both informing and enabling community feedback are required responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empower people
rubrics_metrics.description: Empowers People - Informed people feel that they have some degree of control over their situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective information reduces feelings of helplessness that can lead to anger, petitions, negative media remarks, or disruptive interference with incident management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage people in the effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Engages People in the Effort - Provide or support avenues for individuals and organizations in local communities to get involved in the incident management effort in meaningful ways (e.g., volunteering).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use opportunities to channel community willingness to help into constructive roles that assist incident management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish links/relationships with communities
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishes Links or Relationships Between Agencies and Communities for the Duration of the Incident and for the Future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incidents bring diverse people together; effective community information/involvement can strengthen or repair agency-community relationships beyond the incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Help people express feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: Helps People Express Their Feelings - Recognize a wide range of emotions (fear, anxiety, anger, confusion, gratitude, etc.) in affected community members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledging emotions and providing channels for expression is part of effective community relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate agency concern and competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrates Agency Concern, Responsibility, and Competence - Reassure individuals and organizations that incident managers understand community values (property, landmarks, economy, air quality, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear demonstration of concern and understanding builds credibility and trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize community uniqueness
rubrics_metrics.description: All communities are different and will require different outreach and involvement strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid one-size-fits-all approaches; tailor tactics to local conditions and cultures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide accurate, timely, detailed information
rubrics_metrics.description: People who live, work, and play in affected communities need accurate, timely, detailed information about incidents that are impacting them or may impact them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information should be current and specific; timeliness and detail reduce uncertainty and rumor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan for stress and tension
rubrics_metrics.description: Good outreach and involvement strategies recognize and plan for the fact that incidents create a high degree of stress and tension within and among communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design communications and meetings with heightened emotions in mind; anticipate and mitigate tensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involvement aids recovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Affected communities recover best when individuals and organizations are involved in some way in incident management activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where feasible, provide meaningful roles or avenues for community participation to aid recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for diverse community needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Communities consist of a variety of individuals and groups that often have different needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify subgroups and tailor messages and channels accordingly (e.g., renters vs. homeowners, businesses, special interest groups).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use incidents to educate about agency programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Incidents provide opportunities to educate communities about other agency programs and activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage outreach to inform communities about available services and longer-term programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: General rules for positive relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Be flexible; Listen, listen, listen; Prepare to meet community members on their turf; Make personnel available to answer their questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical interpersonal rules—prioritize listening, accessibility, and adaptability; these are core to building trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earn credibility with community members
rubrics_metrics.description: Always try to make sure they hear it from you first; Always involve community members when giving out information; Follow through on commitments and monitor Information staff commitments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistently proactive, inclusive, and reliable communication establishes credibility. Do your best to keep the community well informed with the most up to date information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community analysis requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a clear understanding of any existing agency/community relations and perceptions and understand the community well enough to accurately forecast incident effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment of perceptions and vulnerabilities is essential for designing outreach and anticipating impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify community resources for communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Document community resources such as local gathering places, locations people depend on to get news, broadcast/print media, meeting facilities, and frequently visited locations (post office, grocery stores, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These resources are useful for disseminating information and setting up outreach points (e.g., kiosks, bulletin boards).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify key individuals and organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify communities directly affected and key individuals/organizations (landowners; homeowners & HOAs; other residents; business owners; elected officials; community leaders; special interest groups).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local agency personnel and Agency Administrator/Executive may provide lists; keeping these stakeholders informed prevents conflicts and problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working with elected officials—responsibility and coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether working with elected officials is your responsibility (check Transition Meeting); find out your role (Agency Administrator usually answers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roles vary—PIO may meet regularly with elected officials, provide briefing materials/support, monitor activities, share responsibilities with Area Commands/MAC groups, and gather contact information for local office representatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate with officials' other offices
rubrics_metrics.description: If the official has other offices, keep them informed also.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain broad outreach to all relevant offices to ensure consistent information flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notify leadership and involve security for official interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Notify Incident Commander and Agency Administrator/Executive to create a feedback loop; involve security personnel when coordinating officials' visits or briefings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure coordination and safety for VIPs; PIO may prepare itinerary, briefing materials, arrange transportation, obtain PPE, arrange news conferences, and provide advice/counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to hold a news conference
rubrics_metrics.description: Decision triggers include: release of new totals (structures lost/saved, resource allocations); determination of cause; occurrence of a significant incident-within-the-incident (serious injury/etc.); desire of a visiting dignitary to comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these criteria to judge the necessity of a formal press conference rather than other communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan steps for a news conference
rubrics_metrics.description: Get Incident Commander's approval; contact dignitary's press person; select site; notify media of time/place/purpose and speakers; prepare handouts and agendas; designate a facilitator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Site selection considerations include proximity to action (without interfering), capacity for media, speaker placement, background/lighting, and power access; ensure ADA compliance (sign language interpreter available). Facilitator should explain ground rules, introduce speakers, keep the briefing moving and coordinate Q&A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conducting community relations activities—use multiple tools/networks
rubrics_metrics.description: After identifying affected communities and key stakeholders, decide how to communicate using a variety of tools and techniques; existing information networks often work best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local agency personnel can advise on credible ways to reach specific audiences; use multiple tools to reach different groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement community relations plan—practical tips
rubrics_metrics.description: Set up a liaison between the community and Incident Command Post; use local transportation resources; be perceptive and empathetic; set up a community contact to help disseminate information; use local facilities for meetings; keep community leaders informed of serious changes that affect the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize outreach via designated contacts and local infrastructure; empathy and timely updates are emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-way communication tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Tools include social media (Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn), Neighborhood Information Centers, unstaffed information kiosks/bulletin boards at strategic locations, fact sheets and maps (updated frequently), programs for local cable television, and Internet sites/QR codes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One-way tools are used to disseminate incident information widely and can be updated as needed (daily or twice daily). Consider posting at grocery stores, post offices, libraries, banks, churches, roadblocks, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-way communication tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Tools include individual contacts and visits, town hall meetings, community/civic organization meetings, school programs, and special community events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two-way methods allow communities to express needs and concerns and let PIOs receive input; town halls must be well designed, planned, and facilitated because large meetings can be risky when emotions run high.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relay community feedback to IMT
rubrics_metrics.description: Gather information about community perceptions of the incident management effort; rumors circulating; specific local concerns or issues; local political sensitivities; and provide recommendations about how the Incident Commander and personnel should respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regularly report back to IMT and recommend responses; reporting back to individuals/organizations that raised issues builds credibility for the IMT and agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get individuals and organizations involved
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct or support volunteer efforts; provide tours of the incident base and incident to educate the public and gain support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Volunteers can assist with outreach and logistics; tours can educate and increase public understanding but should be managed for safety and messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize early signs of a strained community situation
rubrics_metrics.description: Single focus on another event (destruction of homes, road closures, excess smoke), extreme agitation, 'big person syndrome' (need to be in charge), community's unreasonable expectations of incident personnel, sudden negative changes in temperament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train students/PIOs to recognize these indicators so they can escalate outreach and apply de-escalation/engagement strategies early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triggers for heightened community relations effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Heightened outreach needed when: incident threatens or impacts populated areas; in the event of deaths or serious injuries; when major travel corridors are closed or restricted; when rumors, political concerns, or community actions hamper incident operations; when communities can take action to prepare for or prevent damage during an expanding incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these triggers to scale up community relations activities and outreach resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community meetings caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Community meetings can be useful but are a double-edged sword; they can be rough, especially if there is negative history between the community and your agency. Gauge temperament and do analysis first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If emotions are high, design, plan, and facilitate meetings carefully; prepare to handle mob mentality and rabble-rousers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare for special situations (incidents-within-an-incident)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preparation is the key: have basic plans (boilerplates), continually update plans, know agency procedures, understand you may be talking to victims' families, know the agency system for benefits/family liaison, and request experienced PIO help when necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If predictable, it is preventable. Do not hesitate to request additional experienced PIOs for serious special situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know lead agency policies for special situations
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure you know the lead agency's policies regarding handling special situations and release of information to media and public; discuss policy with your reporting Public Information Officer, Incident Commander, or Agency Administrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reach agreement ahead of time about your role in a special situation—policies vary by agency and incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess the incident for special situations
rubrics_metrics.description: Key assessment questions: scale of incident; rarity; visibility; expected duration; jurisdiction of the incident-within-the-incident; who is affected and whether prominent people are involved; proximity to news media; competing news stories; whether an investigation has been initiated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these questions to craft the communications plan and predict media/political interest and required resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess staff capacity and skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide if another PIO is needed; determine if you have enough people and the right experience/skills (can they give interviews?); order more people if necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staff assessment should consider experience levels and ability to represent the agency appropriately under scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make assignments for special situations
rubrics_metrics.description: Make assignments addressing media, public, politicians, incident personnel/internal audiences; assess facilities (size, communications, location, accessibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly assign responsibilities and check facility suitability for briefings, press events, and liaison functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special Situations Plan considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan should consider agency policies, release approvals (e.g., releasing accident victims' names), home base communications, conflicts between agencies/public, monitoring rumors/media/social media, evacuations (special groups if approved), and VIP visits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document approval chains and sensitive-release protocols; include protocols for rumor monitoring and interagency conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain and update the plan regularly
rubrics_metrics.description: Write the plan and regularly update it—review at least once each Operational Period and change as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plans should be living documents adjusted to evolving incident conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilitating media interviews—sensitivity and compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Be sensitive: understand some people want to talk while others do not; work with local PIO/PAO; respect local customs; ask what the sensitive issues are; ensure HIPAA compliance; prepare witnesses/survivors for interviews (what they cannot talk about; they may need help leaving interviews; they may be legally barred from speaking); gently obtain a written fact sheet from the family; know your agency policy and delegation of authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protect privacy and legal constraints; prepare interviewees carefully to avoid inadvertent disclosures; coordinate with legal/liaison staff as needed.
